source.question: Why did F-12's oil rate jump after the December 2014 shutdown?

note: Oct 28 night: the summary's '77%' rests on E16, warned (poor WOR trend); its sentence has no hedge. Accepted before only because the hedge rule sliced the sentence at masked positions (a bug, fixed).

submission.summary: F-12 was shut in for 32 days from 2014-11-30 to 2014-12-31 (field-wide) [E2]. Its oil rate jumped from 185 Sm3/d to 860 Sm3/d (+366%) on restart [E2], with monthly oil rising to 862 Sm3/d in January 2015 [E4]. The jump coincides with water cut collapsing from 96% to 31% [E4] and wellhead pressure rising from 32.4 bar to 71.0 bar [E4] while the choke was cut to 30% [E4] and liquid fell 77% [E5][E4], indicating the well had been producing mostly water at capacity and the shut-in let water segregate/pressure rebuild so oil could take the limited liquid rate.

findings.claim: F-12 was shut in 32 days from 2014-11-30 to 2014-12-31; oil rate per producing day was 185 Sm3/d before and 860 Sm3/d after, a 366% increase.
Monthly average confirms the jump: November 2014 oil rate 186 Sm3/d rose to 862 Sm3/d in January 2015, an increase of 677 Sm3/d.
Water cut collapsed from 96% in June 2014 to 31% in January 2015, a drop of 65.3 percentage points, and water volume fell 92% from 152035 Sm3 to 11588 Sm3.

Liquid rate fell 77% from 5354 Sm3/d in June 2014 to 1251 Sm3/d in January 2015 while choke was reduced from 97% to 30% and wellhead pressure rose from 32.4 bar to 71.0 bar, showing oil increased even though total liquid was choked back.

The pattern is consistent with a waterflood well that had been at 100% choke producing 97% water at the platform liquid limit; the 32-day shut-in allowed near-wellbore water to recede and pressure to rebuild (WHP 131 bar during shut-in), so after restart oil could occupy the constrained liquid rate at much lower water cut. The December 2014 shut-in has no data flag other than the long-standing BHP sensor failure since 2010.
